claim: Among the top 10,000 Twitch streamers by revenue, the median monthly on-platform payout was $1,665, while the top 100 averaged $49,821/month and the top 10 averaged $155,323/month.
stance_target: Creator income is extremely right-skewed even within the elite tier, so median-vs-mean gaps understate inequality unless the non-earning majority is included.
scope_conditions: Twitch on-platform payouts only (subscriptions, bits, ads); excludes sponsorships and external revenue, which the cited source says make up a far greater share of a streamer's total income. Derived from the October 2021 Twitch payout data leak, covering Aug 2019 - Oct 2021. Only the top 10,000 by revenue — i.e. an already-selected elite, out of 657,504 affiliates and 29,707 partners on the platform in 2019.
quoted_support: A 2021 leak of payouts by Twitch (Needleman, 2021; Twitch.tv, 2021) to the top ten thousand streamers by revenue revealed median monthly payouts of 1,665$, rising to 49,821$ for the 100 largest streamers and 155,323$ for the top ten and these direct payments do not include any external revenue sources (such as payments from promotional activities) that make up a far greater share of a streamer's total income (D'Anastasio, 2021).
region: Global Twitch platform; leak is not broken out by country. Predominantly US/Western streamers by volume.

claim: Newcomer Twitch streamers who reached only affiliate status reverted their total streaming time to pre-pandemic levels within roughly 4-8 weeks, while newcomers who reached partner status sustained the elevated level — effort persistence was conditional on early monetization feedback.
stance_target: Creators disengage quickly when early platform feedback signals low income potential; attrition of effort is measurable within two months of the market signal.
scope_conditions: Twitch newcomer subsample (streamers first appearing after January 2020), 66,786 streamer-week observations, weeks 5-29 of 2020; status measured 23 Jan and 25 Jun 2020. Difference-in-differences with week and language fixed effects.
quoted_support: However, when in late spring case numbers were falling while lockdown policies were lifted and mobility increased again, new affiliates quickly started to reduce their streaming time down to pre-COVID-19 levels, while streamers who gained partner status stabilized their streaming time at a higher level.
numbers: new affiliates 15.4% below new partners (POST x TREAT = -0.154, p<0.01)
region: Global Twitch sample with language fixed effects; identification rests on Western lockdown timing

claim: Streamers who never progressed beyond standard (unmonetized) status showed no measurable behavioural response to the pandemic and invested little time from the outset, which the authors read as evidence they never intended to professionalize.
stance_target: A large share of nominally 'active' creators are hobbyists whose inclusion in any denominator inflates apparent attrition rates and deflates apparent income.
scope_conditions: Twitch newcomers, Jan-Jul 2020; status categories assigned by Twitch, an unobserved subjective component in the partner decision.
quoted_support: In contrast, users who remained standard users seemed to be completely unaffected (and are not considered in the following). ... those newcomers who remained standard users neither showed a similar reaction, nor did they put in a large time investment in the first place.

claim: Twitch's affiliate (first monetization) threshold requires 50 followers, 500 total broadcast minutes across 7 unique days, and an average of 3 or more concurrent viewers in the prior 30 days.
stance_target: The measurable floor for 'time to first income' on Twitch is set by an explicit, low, published platform threshold — but affiliate status yields only partial monetization.
scope_conditions: Twitch policy as documented in 2020 (Twitch.tv 2020a). Partner status, which unlocks full monetization, adds undisclosed subjective criteria.
quoted_support: As of today, to be invited for affiliate status, streamers need to have at least 50 followers as well as to have broadcasted more than 500 min in total, on seven unique days, with an average of three or more concurrent viewers in the last 30 days (Twitch.tv, 2020a).

claim: Across 18,467 Twitch streamers, mean stream length was 259.7 minutes (median 240.4) before COVID and 272.3 minutes (median 255.2) after, with mean total time streamed per streamer rising from 7,110 to 8,343 minutes over the study window.
stance_target: Content creation as an occupation demands large, measurable time inputs — roughly 4-4.5 hours per broadcast session, before any promotional or administrative work.
scope_conditions: 18,467 individual Twitch streamers, 1,936,528 unique streams, drawn from 3,329,042 hourly top-500 observations, 2 Aug 2019 - 30 Jul 2020. Pre-period = weeks 5-10 of 2020; post-period = weeks 12-29. Channels operated by organisations ('studio', 'official') and gambling channels excluded; streams over 24h dropped.
region: Global Twitch, language fixed effects; no Southeast Asia breakout

claim: Newcomer Twitch streamers increased average broadcast length by 13.0% relative to the established-partner control group after lockdown, roughly eight times the 1.7% increase shown by established non-partner streamers.
stance_target: Time investment in content creation is highly elastic to opportunity cost, and the least-established creators are the most elastic.
scope_conditions: DiD on log(stream length), 1,936,528 observations, week and language fixed effects, robust SEs. Control = pre-pandemic Twitch partners (n=8,839); Treatment 1 = pre-pandemic affiliates/standard (n=5,615); Treatment 2 = newcomers entering after Jan 2020 (n=4,013).
quoted_support: In particular, for treatment group 1 the estimate of 0.017 suggests that length was on average 1.7% higher in the post-pandemic period relative to the streaming length in the control group, whereas for treatment group 2, the post-period growth in streaming length was almost eight times higher with an estimate of 0.130 equaling to an additional increase of 13.0%.
region: Global Twitch; authors concede they do not account for country-specific lockdown policy or time zones and rely on Western mobility comparability

claim: The Twitch panel's sampling frame required at least one hourly top-500 placement (a floor of about 21 concurrent viewers), which the authors concede introduces survivorship bias while arguing the low floor mitigates it.
stance_target: That measured-telemetry creator panels are free of survivorship bias.
scope_conditions: Applies to Wollborn et al.'s 18,467-streamer panel; the authors state Twitch 'boasts millions of regular streamers' but deliberately exclude casual and one-time streamers as unrepresentative of professionalizing behaviour.
quoted_support: Thus, using only the top 500 live streams at first glance might give the impression of only covering the most successful streamers and that the resulting sample could thus suffer from survivorship bias, the low minimum viewer threshold of 21 shows that many streamers in our sample are far from what one would call successful.

claim: Twitch held 63.59% of live-streaming hours watched in February 2020 (979,968,010 hours) rising to 66.82% by June 2020 (1,553,283,931 hours), ahead of YouTube Gaming Live (22.81% falling to 20.29%), Facebook Gaming (11.93% / 11.56%) and Mixer (1.66% / 1.33%).
stance_target: Platform concentration context for interpreting single-platform creator studies.
scope_conditions: Streamlabs vendor telemetry (Streamlabs 2020a, 2020b), gaming-oriented live streaming only; excludes TikTok, Bigo Live, Nimo TV and other platforms dominant in Southeast Asia.
region: Global, but Western-platform-centric; SEA-dominant platforms absent

claim: Median total views per Twitch streamer over the study window were 1,864 pre-COVID and 2,603 post-COVID, against means of 9,374 and 13,907 — a mean-to-median ratio of roughly 5.0x and 5.3x.
stance_target: Audience (and therefore income) distribution among creators is so skewed that mean figures are structurally misleading; the median creator has a small fraction of the average creator's reach.
scope_conditions: 18,467 Twitch streamers, weeks 5-29 of 2020. Note that this is already a filtered sample of streamers who cleared the 21-concurrent-viewer bar at least once; the true platform-wide skew is more extreme.
